claim: EGFR is mutated or overexpressed in a variety of human cancers.
source: Because EGFR is mutated or overexpressed in a variety of human cancers, it has become a major prognostic marker and therapeutic target (Grandis and Sok, 2004; Herbst et al., 2004; Nicholson et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition of EGFR has been a successful strategy for the treatment of patients with non-small-cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) expressing mutant EGFR.
source: Pharmacologic inhibition of EGFR has been a successful strategy for the treatment of patients with non-small-cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) expressing mutant EGFR (Lee, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Therapies targeting wild-type EGFR in tumors such as head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) have been less effective due to intrinsic and acquired tumor resistance to EGFR inhibitors.
source: However, therapies targeting wild-type EGFR in tumors such as head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) have been less effective due to intrinsic and acquired tumor resistance to EGFR inhibitors (Leemans et al., 2011; Rieke et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: EGFR may be activated by seven different ligands that bind the extracellular domain of the receptor with varying affinity.
source: EGFR may be activated by seven different ligands that bind the extracellular domain of the receptor with varying affinity (Singh et al., 2016; Roepstorff et al., 2009; Ebner and Derynck, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: EGFR ligands are synthetized as transmembrane precursors that undergo proteolysis by metalloproteases at the cell surface to produce functional soluble molecules.
source: These ligands are synthetized as transmembrane precursors that undergo proteolysis by metalloproteases at the cell surface to produce functional soluble molecules (Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Ectodomain 'shedding' is proposed to be the rate-limiting step of the molecular processing that determines the concentration of a mature ligand in vivo.
source: Ectodomain 'shedding' is proposed to be the rate-limiting step of the molecular processing that determines the concentration of a mature ligand in vivo (Peschon et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Ligand binding leads to EGFR dimerization and the activation of its tyrosine kinase.
source: Ligand binding leads to EGFR dimerization and the activation of its tyrosine kinase (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Phosphorylation of tyrosine residues in the carboxyl-terminus of EGFR provides docking sites for proteins with SH2 and PTB domains, which trigger signal transduction through multiple pathways.
source: Subsequent phosphorylation of tyrosine residues in the carboxyl-terminus of EGFR provides docking sites for proteins with SH2 and PTB domains, which trigger signal transduction through Ras-Raf-mitogen-activated protein kinase/extracellular-signal regulated kinase 1/2 (MAPK/ERK1/2), phosphoinositide 3-kinase, AKT, Src family kinases (SFKs), STATs, phospholipase Cγ1, Rho family GTPases and other pathways (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Once ligand-bound, EGFR is rapidly endocytosed via clathrin-dependent and -independent mechanisms.
source: Once ligand-bound, EGFR is rapidly endocytosed via clathrin-dependent and -independent mechanisms (Sorkin and Goh, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: EGFR-ligand complexes may recycle back to the plasma membrane from early and sorting endosomes but are also efficiently targeted to lysosomes for degradation.
source: Subsequently, EGFR-ligand complexes may recycle back to the plasma membrane from early and sorting endosomes but are also efficiently targeted to lysosomes for degradation (Sorkin and Goh, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Recruitment of E3 ubiquitin ligases, the Cbl proteins (c-Cbl and Cbl-b), to activated EGFR is a key event leading to receptor ubiquitylation.
source: Recruitment of E3 ubiquitin ligases, the Cbl proteins (c-Cbl and Cbl-b), to activated EGFR is a key event leading to receptor ubiquitylation (Levkowitz et al., 1998; Levkowitz et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Ubiquitylation of the receptor and its binding to the clathrin adaptor AP-2 serve as two redundant mechanisms for receptor recruitment into clathrin-coated pits.
source: Ubiquitylation of the receptor and its binding to the clathrin adaptor AP-2 serve as two redundant mechanisms for receptor recruitment into clathrin-coated pits (Fortian et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Poly-ubiquitylation mediates binding of EGFR to ESCRT proteins in sorting endosomes leading to the incorporation of the receptor into intraluminal vesicles of multi-vesicular endosomes and subsequent lysosomal degradation.
source: Poly-ubiquitylation also mediates binding of EGFR to ESCRT proteins in sorting endosomes leading to the incorporation of the receptor into intraluminal vesicles of multi-vesicular endosomes and subsequent lysosomal degradation (Eden et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Activation of <10,000 EGFRs per cell with low ligand concentrations (<1–2 ng/ml) results in EGFR internalization specifically via the clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) pathway.
source: Activation of <10,000 EGFRs per cell with low ligand concentrations (<1–2 ng/ml) results in EGFR internalization specifically via the clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) pathway, whereas at higher EGF concentrations the process becomes largely clathrin independent (CIE), presumably, due to saturation of the CME pathway (Lund et al., 1990; Jiang and Sorkin, 2003; Sigismund et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: At higher EGF concentrations the endocytosis process becomes largely clathrin independent (CIE), presumably, due to saturation of the CME pathway.
source: Activation of <10,000 EGFRs per cell with low ligand concentrations (<1–2 ng/ml) results in EGFR internalization specifically via the clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) pathway, whereas at higher EGF concentrations the process becomes largely clathrin independent (CIE), presumably, due to saturation of the CME pathway (Lund et al., 1990; Jiang and Sorkin, 2003; Sigismund et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and speculation about mechanism

claim: A ligand concentration threshold was observed in EGFR ubiquitylation.
source: Furthermore, a ligand concentration threshold was observed in EGFR ubiquitylation (Sigismund et al., 2008; Sigismund et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: At low EGF concentrations (1–2 ng/ml) activated EGFRs are not ubiquitylated in HeLa cells, and therefore, not efficiently targeted to lysosomes, which leads to continued recycling and signaling.
source: It has been proposed that at low EGF concentrations (1–2 ng/ml) activated EGFRs are not ubiquitylated in HeLa cells, and therefore, not efficiently targeted to lysosomes, which leads to continued recycling and signaling (Sigismund et al., 2008; Sigismund et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Endosomal sorting of EGFR is rapid in the presence of low EGF concentrations but is saturated by high ligand concentrations in B82 mouse fibroblasts.
source: Importantly though, previous studies in B82 mouse fibroblasts have shown that endosomal sorting of EGFR is rapid in the presence of low EGF concentrations but is saturated by high ligand concentrations (French et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: A small pool of ligand-occupied EGFRs is sufficient to fully activate the ERK1/2 signaling pathway in several types of cultured cells.
source: Furthermore, a small pool of ligand-occupied EGFRs was shown to be sufficient to fully activate the ERK1/2 signaling pathway in several types of cultured cells, in contrast to other downstream signaling pathways which demand high EGFR ligand concentrations before significant activation is apparent (Albeck et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2016; Krall et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Other downstream signaling pathways demand high EGFR ligand concentrations before significant activation is apparent.
source: Furthermore, a small pool of ligand-occupied EGFRs was shown to be sufficient to fully activate the ERK1/2 signaling pathway in several types of cultured cells, in contrast to other downstream signaling pathways which demand high EGFR ligand concentrations before significant activation is apparent (Albeck et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2016; Krall et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The concentration of EGFR ligands in human body fluids and tumors is typically below 1–2 ng/ml, with the exception of breast milk, saliva and urine.
source: The concentration of EGFR ligands in human body fluids and tumors is typically below 1–2 ng/ml, with the exception of breast milk, saliva and urine, fluids where EGF is more abundant though inaccessible to EGFRs (Ishikawa et al., 2005; Rich et al., 2017; Dvorak, 2010; Connolly and Rose, 1988; Murdoch-Kinch et al., 2011; Hirata and Orth, 1979; Oka and Orth, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: HSC3 cells have five copies of the wild-type EGFR gene and express ~5×10^5 EGFRs per cell.
source: These HNSCC cells have five copies of the wild-type EGFR gene (canSar v3.0) and thus express ~5×105 EGFRs per cell, which is 5–10-fold higher than EGFR levels in normal keratinocytes and fibroblasts.
evidence: Supported by reference to database and inference about expression levels

claim: HSC3 cells express 5–10-fold higher EGFR levels than normal keratinocytes and fibroblasts.
source: These HNSCC cells have five copies of the wild-type EGFR gene (canSar v3.0) and thus express ~5×105 EGFRs per cell, which is 5–10-fold higher than EGFR levels in normal keratinocytes and fibroblasts.
evidence: Supported by inference from gene copy number data

claim: HSC3 cells produce tumors in athymic nude mice.
source: HSC3 cells produce tumors in athymic nude mice (Momose et al., 1989; Kudo et al., 2003), and the growth of HSC3 tumor xenografts is inhibited by blocking EGFR activity, indicating that these tumors are EGFR-dependent (Kudo et al., 2003; Shintani et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The growth of HSC3 tumor xenografts is inhibited by blocking EGFR activity, indicating that these tumors are EGFR-dependent.
source: HSC3 cells produce tumors in athymic nude mice (Momose et al., 1989; Kudo et al., 2003), and the growth of HSC3 tumor xenografts is inhibited by blocking EGFR activity, indicating that these tumors are EGFR-dependent (Kudo et al., 2003; Shintani et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Overexpression of EGFR is observed in the majority of human HNSCC.
source: Because overexpression of EGFR is observed in the majority of human HNSCC (Leemans et al., 2011; Rieke et al., 2016; Grandis and Tweardy, 1992), HSC3 cells is considered to be a suitable model to recapitulate human EGFR-dependent head-and-neck carcinoma.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: HSC3 cells are considered to be a suitable model to recapitulate human EGFR-dependent head-and-neck carcinoma.
source: Because overexpression of EGFR is observed in the majority of human HNSCC (Leemans et al., 2011; Rieke et al., 2016; Grandis and Tweardy, 1992), HSC3 cells is considered to be a suitable model to recapitulate human EGFR-dependent head-and-neck carcinoma.
evidence: Supported by inference from EGFR overexpression data and citations

claim: EGFR was tagged with eGFP in HSC3 cells using a zinc-finger nuclease (ZFN)-based genome-editing method.
source: To enable direct visualization of endogenous EGFR in tumor cells in vivo, EGFR was tagged with eGFP in HSC3 cells using a zinc-finger nuclease (ZFN)-based genome-editing method (Doyon et al., 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to published method and schematic in Figure 1A

claim: After two cycles of gene-editing and multiple rounds of clonal selection, EGFR-GFP constituted 40–50% of total cellular EGFR protein in several clonal pools of HSC3 cells.
source: After two cycles of gene-editing and multiple rounds of clonal selection, several clonal pools of HSC3 cells (single HSC3 cells do not survive) were obtained, in which EGFR-GFP constituted 40–50% of total cellular EGFR protein (Figure 1B–D), indicating that 2–3 copies of EGFR gene were edited.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B-D

claim: 2–3 copies of EGFR gene were edited in HSC3/EGFR-GFP cells.
source: After two cycles of gene-editing and multiple rounds of clonal selection, several clonal pools of HSC3 cells (single HSC3 cells do not survive) were obtained, in which EGFR-GFP constituted 40–50% of total cellular EGFR protein (Figure 1B–D), indicating that 2–3 copies of EGFR gene were edited.
evidence: Inferred from the proportion of EGFR-GFP to total EGFR shown in Figure 1B-D

claim: The dose dependency of EGFR phosphorylation at Tyr1068 on EGF concentration is essentially the same between HSC3/EGFR-GFP and the parental HSC3 cells.
source: The dose dependency of EGFR phosphorylation at Tyr1068 and EGFR ubiquitylation on EGF concentration was essentially the same between HSC3/EGFR-GFP and the parental HSC3 cells (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D

claim: The dose dependency of EGFR ubiquitylation on EGF concentration is essentially the same between HSC3/EGFR-GFP and the parental HSC3 cells.
source: The dose dependency of EGFR phosphorylation at Tyr1068 and EGFR ubiquitylation on EGF concentration was essentially the same between HSC3/EGFR-GFP and the parental HSC3 cells (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D

claim: When HSC3/EGFR-GFP cells were stimulated with EGF-Rhodamine (EGF-Rh), efficient endocytosis of EGF-Rh:EGFR-GFP complexes was observed with 80–90% of these complexes accumulating in endosomes after 12 min.
source: When HSC3/EGFR-GFP cells were stimulated with EGF-Rhodamine (EGF-Rh), efficient endocytosis of EGF-Rh:EGFR-GFP complexes was observed in living cells as evidenced by the accumulation of 80–90% of these complexes in endosomes with only a minimal EGF-Rh presence at the cell surface after 12 min of continuous endocytosis (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Subcutaneous grafting of HSC3/EGFR-GFP cells into the flanks of athymic nude mice led to tumor formation.
source: Subcutaneous (s.q.) grafting of HSC3/EGFR-GFP cells into the flanks of athymic nude mice led to tumor formation (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Treatment of mice harboring HSC3/EGFR-GFP tumor xenografts with gefitinib substantially reduced tumor growth.
source: Treatment of mice harboring HSC3/EGFR-GFP tumor xenografts with gefitinib, a small-molecule EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, substantially reduced tumor growth, demonstrating that HSC3/EGFR-GFP tumors require EGFR tyrosine kinase activity to sustain tumorigenesis (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F

claim: HSC3/EGFR-GFP tumors require EGFR tyrosine kinase activity to sustain tumorigenesis.
source: Treatment of mice harboring HSC3/EGFR-GFP tumor xenografts with gefitinib, a small-molecule EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, substantially reduced tumor growth, demonstrating that HSC3/EGFR-GFP tumors require EGFR tyrosine kinase activity to sustain tumorigenesis (Figure 1F).
evidence: Inferred from gefitinib treatment data shown in Figure 1F

claim: The GFP tag does not affect EGFR function.
source: Together, these data confirm that the GFP tag does not affect EGFR function, and validate HSC3/EGFR-GFP cells as an appropriate experimental system to study EGFR signaling and trafficking in EGFR-dependent tumors in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from multiple functional assays shown in Figure 1

claim: The bulk of EGFR-GFP in HSC3/EGFR-GFP flank xenografts is located at the plasma membrane.
source: The bulk of EGFR-GFP was found to be located at the plasma membrane (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 2A-B

claim: Clusters and/or vesicles containing EGFR-GFP, as well as their movement, appearance and disappearance, were occasionally observed in cells located at the periphery of tumor nodules.
source: Clusters and/or vesicles containing EGFR-GFP, as well as their movement, appearance and disappearance, were occasionally observed in cells located at the periphery of tumor nodules (Figure 2A–B; Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 2A-B and videos

claim: GFP-positive puncta did not display significant motility in vivo, in contrast to the rapid movement of endosomes typically observed in cultured cells.
source: Of note, the GFP-positive puncta did not display significant motility in vivo, in contrast to thhe rapid movement of endosomes typically observed in cultured cells.
evidence: Observation from intravital imaging compared to known behavior in cultured cells

claim: Confocal imaging of tumor cryosections demonstrates a predominantly plasma membrane localization for EGFR-GFP.
source: Large-area montage images of the tumor section demonstrate a predominantly plasma membrane localization for EGFR-GFP (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Intracellular GFP puncta were detected in a limited fraction of cells in the tumor.
source: Intracellular GFP puncta were detected in a limited fraction of cells in the tumor (insets in Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Many GFP-positive clusters/vesicles contain early endosome antigen 1 (EEA.1), suggesting that this pool of EGFR-GFP is located in early/sorting endosomes.
source: Many GFP-positive clusters/vesicles, including those that are proximal to the plasma membrane, contained early endosome antigen 1 (EEA.1), suggesting that this pool of EGFR-GFP is located in early/sorting endosomes (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 3A and inference about endosome identity

claim: The predominantly peripheral location of endosomes and their low motility is considered to be due to dense packing of cells in tumor nodules limiting the cytoplasmic volume in these cells.
source: The predominantly peripheral location of endosomes and their low motility is considered to be due to dense packing of cells in tumor nodules limiting the cytoplasmic volume in these cells as can be seen in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: Inference based on observation of cell packing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The localization pattern for the total EGFR (untagged and GFP-tagged EGFR) is essentially identical to that seen for EGFR-GFP.
source: Staining of tumor sections with EGFR antibodies demonstrated a localization pattern for the total EGFR (untagged and GFP-tagged EGFR) that is essentially identical to that seen for EGFR-GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), thus confirming that the equivalence of steady-state endocytic trafficking dynamics between untagged EGFR and EGFR-GFP.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The steady-state endocytic trafficking dynamics are equivalent between untagged EGFR and EGFR-GFP.
source: Staining of tumor sections with EGFR antibodies demonstrated a localization pattern for the total EGFR (untagged and GFP-tagged EGFR) that is essentially identical to that seen for EGFR-GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), thus confirming that the equivalence of steady-state endocytic trafficking dynamics between untagged EGFR and EGFR-GFP.
evidence: Inferred from identical localization patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: EGFR-GFP localization in tongue orthotopic xenografts is similar to that observed in flank tumor xenografts.
source: Montage images covering large areas of tumors revealed predominant localization of EGFR-GFP at the cell surface with occasional clusters of GFP in vesicles, a distribution pattern essentially similar to that observed in flank tumors (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Only a small fraction of EGFRs are endocytosed under steady-state growth conditions of HSC3/EGFR-GFP tumor xenografts.
source: Together, the data in Figures 2 and 3A strongly suggest that only a small fraction of EGFRs are endocytosed under steady-state growth conditions of HSC3/EGFR-GFP tumor xenografts (in the presence of endogenous EGFR ligands).
evidence: Inferred from imaging data in Figures 2 and 3A

claim: Phosphorylation of Tyr1068 in EGFR and EGFR-GFP displayed a linear dependence on the concentration of EGF when incubated with cells for 10 min in vitro.
source: In vitro, phosphorylation of Tyr1068 in EGFR and EGFR-GFP (measured as the pY1068/EGFR ratio) displayed a linear dependence on the concentration of EGF when incubated with cells for 10 min (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: When cells were incubated with the same range of EGF concentrations for 12 hr, the extent of Tyr1068 phosphorylation mirrored the results obtained using an acute stimulation.
source: When cells were incubated with the same range of EGF concentrations for 12 hr, the extent of Tyr1068 phosphorylation mirrored the results obtained using an acute stimulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The mean predicted concentrations of EGFR ligands are ~0.2 ng/ml (~34 pM) in flank xenografts and ~0.6 ng/ml (100 pM) in tongue implants.
source: The analysis yielded mean predicted concentrations of EGFR ligands as low as ~0.2 and ~0.6 ng/ml (~34 and 100 pM) in the flank and tongue implants, respectively (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Calculated from in vitro/in vivo comparison of EGFR phosphorylation shown in Figure 4D-E

claim: Immunolabeling of flank tumor xenograft sections with the pY1068 antibody demonstrated EGFR phosphorylation in almost all cells in tumor sections with the predominant localization of the phosphorylated receptor at the plasma membrane.
source: This assumption is technically difficult to test directly with high precision, although immunolabeling of flank tumor xenograft sections with the pY1068 antibody demonstrated EGFR phosphorylation in almost all cells in tumor sections with the predominant localization of the phosphorylated receptor at the plasma membrane (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: The intensity of pY1068 signal was proportional to the intensity of GFP (EGFR-GFP) signal, suggesting the relatively homogenous activation of EGFR within the tumor.
source: The intensity of pY1068 signal was proportional to the intensity of GFP (EGFR-GFP) signal, suggesting the relatively homogenous activation of EGFR within the tumor.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of signal intensities in imaging data

claim: Mean concentrations of EGFR ligands in H322 and MDA-MB-468 tumor xenografts are low, although these concentrations displayed a wider range in MDA-MB-468 tumors.
source: The comparative in vitro/in vivo analysis of the EGFR activity, performed as with HSC3 cells, estimated low EGFR ligand concentrations in xenograft tumors of H322 and MDA-MB-468 cells, although these concentrations displayed a wider range in MDA-MB-468 tumors (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4D-E

claim: Mean concentrations of EGFR ligands in tumor xenografts are 0.1–0.6 ng/ml (17–100 pM).
source: In summary, the in vitro/in vivo calibration analysis of the EGFR activity predicted that mean concentrations of EGFR ligands in tumor xenografts are 0.1–0.6 ng/ml (17–100 pM).
evidence: Summary of data from multiple experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: pY1068/EGFR ratio values measured in human HNSCC specimens were within the range of those values found in mouse tumor xenografts of HSC3/EGFR-GFP cells.
source: Importantly, pY1068/EGFR ratio values measured in human HNSCC specimens were within the range of those values found in mouse tumor xenografts of HSC3/EGFR-GFP cells (Figure 4F–G), suggesting the presence of low EGFR ligand concentrations in human HNSCC.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4F-G

claim: Low EGFR ligand concentrations are present in human HNSCC.
source: Importantly, pY1068/EGFR ratio values measured in human HNSCC specimens were within the range of those values found in mouse tumor xenografts of HSC3/EGFR-GFP cells (Figure 4F–G), suggesting the presence of low EGFR ligand concentrations in human HNSCC.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of pY1068/EGFR ratios shown in Figure 4F-G

claim: MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 phosphorylation reached 75–80% of the maximum phosphorylation in cells stimulated with 0.5 ng/ml (85 pM) EGF.
source: While EGFR phosphorylation at Tyr1068 displayed linear dependence on EGF concentration in the range of 0–5 ng/ml EGF (Figure 5A), MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 phosphorylation reached 75–80% of the maximum phosphorylation in cells stimulated with 0.5 ng/ml (85 pM) EGF (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation of phospholipase C γ1 was marginally stimulated by 0.5–1 ng/ml EGF and increased proportionally to the EGF concentration.
source: In contrast, tyrosine phosphorylation of phospholipase C γ1 was marginally stimulated by 0.5–1 ng/ml EGF and increased proportionally to the EGF concentration, in a manner comparable to that of the pY1068 signal (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Significant phosphorylation of STAT3 was reliably detected only at >1 ng/ml EGF and was proportional to EGF concentrations.
source: Likewise, significant phosphorylation of STAT3 was reliably detected only at >1 ng/ml EGF and was also proportional to EGF concentrations (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Constitutive activity of AKT was high, and EGF stimulation did not lead to a substantial increase of this activity.
source: Constitutive activity of AKT (Figure 5E) and SFKs measured by phosphorylation of their catalytic tyrosines (Figure 5F) was high, and EGF stimulation did not lead to a substantial increase of these activities.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Constitutive activity of SFKs measured by phosphorylation of their catalytic tyrosines was high, and EGF stimulation did not lead to a substantial increase of this activity.
source: Constitutive activity of AKT (Figure 5E) and SFKs measured by phosphorylation of their catalytic tyrosines (Figure 5F) was high, and EGF stimulation did not lead to a substantial increase of these activities.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Similar patterns of EGF-dose-dependence of the major EGFR signaling pathways have been previously observed in several other types of cultured cells.
source: Similar patterns of EGF-dose-dependence of the major EGFR signaling pathways have been previously observed in several other types of cultured cells (Shi et al., 2016; Krall et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The regulation of EGFR-dependent tumor growth in vivo is predominantly driven by signaling through the ERK1/2 pathway.
source: These in vitro data prompted us to hypothesize that the regulation of EGFR-dependent tumor growth in vivo is predominantly driven by signaling through the ERK1/2 pathway.
evidence: Hypothesis based on in vitro dose-response data shown in Figure 5

claim: ERK1/2 phosphorylation in tumors normalized to this phosphorylation in vitro (at 1 ng/ml EGF) was comparable with the normalized phosphorylation of EGFR at Tyr1068.
source: ERK1/2 phosphorylation in tumors normalized to this phosphorylation in vitro (at 1 ng/ml EGF) was comparable with the normalized phosphorylation of EGFR at Tyr1068 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G

claim: In vivo/in vitro ratios of phosphorylation of other signaling effectors, especially STAT3, were significantly higher than these ratios of EGFR and ERK1/2.
source: By contrast, in vivo/in vitro ratios of phosphorylation of other signaling effectors, especially STAT3, were significantly higher than these ratios of EGFR and ERK1/2 (Figure 5G), which may be attributable to EGFR-independent activation of the former pathways in HSC3/EGFR-GFP cells in tumors in vivo, and possibly, detection of phosphoproteins in mouse cells contaminating tumor samples.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G with speculation about mechanism

claim: The ERK1/2 pathway is primarily EGFR-driven in vivo and important for EGFR-dependent tumorigenesis.
source: Overall, the data in Figure 5 support the model whereby the ERK1/2 pathway is primarily EGFR-driven in vivo and important for EGFR-dependent tumorigenesis, whereas multiple other signaling pathways are largely involved in EGFR-independent tumor growth.
evidence: Inferred from data in Figure 5

claim: Multiple other signaling pathways are largely involved in EGFR-independent tumor growth.
source: Overall, the data in Figure 5 support the model whereby the ERK1/2 pathway is primarily EGFR-driven in vivo and important for EGFR-dependent tumorigenesis, whereas multiple other signaling pathways are largely involved in EGFR-independent tumor growth.
evidence: Inferred from data in Figure 5

claim: EGF-Rh could be detected in flank and tongue tumor xenografts ~1 hr after tail vein injection.
source: EGF-Rh could be detected in flank and tongue tumor xenografts ~1 hr after tail vein injection.
evidence: Observation from experimental procedure

claim: The pY1068/EGFR ratio in flank tumors was increased 2.5-fold after EGF-Rh administration.
source: The pY1068/EGFR ratio in flank tumors was increased 2.5-fold after EGF-Rh administration (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The total concentration of EGFR ligands in the presence of systemic EGF-Rh is estimated to be lower than 1–2 ng/ml.
source: Considering the range of endogenous ligand concentrations predicted in Figure 4, the total concentration of EGFR ligands in the presence of systemic EGF-Rh is estimated to be lower than 1–2 ng/ml.
evidence: Inferred from endogenous ligand concentration estimates and EGF-Rh response

claim: Intravital imaging of flank tumor xenografts after EGF-Rh injection revealed co-localization of EGFR-GFP and EGF-Rh in perinuclear vesicles and clusters located proximally or overlapping with the plasma membrane.
source: Intravital imaging of flank tumor xenografts after EGF-Rh injection revealed co-localization of EGFR-GFP and EGF-Rh in perinuclear vesicles and clusters located proximally or overlapping with the plasma membrane (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The motility of EGF-Rh/EGFR-GFP vesicles is very limited when compared with what is typically observed in vitro.
source: Similar to that observed in the absence of EGF-Rh, time-lapse imaging showed that the motility of EGF-Rh/EGFR-GFP vesicles is very limited when compared with what is typically observed in vitro.
evidence: Observation from time-lapse imaging compared to known behavior in vitro

claim: Imaging of EGF-Rh and EGFR-GFP fluorescence on flank tumor sections demonstrated the presence of vesicles containing both ligand and receptor in a large population of cells.
source: Imaging of EGF-Rh and EGFR-GFP fluorescence on flank tumor sections demonstrated the presence of vesicles containing both ligand and receptor in a large population of cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 6C

claim: EGF-Rh had access to EGFR in at least 40–50% of the cells in flank tumors.
source: Quantitation of cells containing EGF-Rh-positive vesicles on multiple sections from different tumors revealed that EGF-Rh had access to EGFR in at least 40–50% of the cells in these tumors.
evidence: Quantification of imaging data from tumor sections

claim: In most cells, EGF-Rh was detected predominantly in endosomes and was essentially absent in the plasma membrane, indicative of a fast and efficient endocytosis.
source: In most cells, EGF-Rh was detected predominantly in endosomes and was essentially absent in the plasma membrane, indicative of a fast and efficient endocytosis (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C with inference about endocytosis efficiency

claim: The accumulation of EGF-Rh in endosomes was increased in clusters of cells at the periphery of tumor nodules, presumably in the vicinity of blood vessels.
source: The accumulation of EGF-Rh in endosomes was increased in clusters of cells at the periphery of tumor nodules, presumably in the vicinity of blood vessels (see large area montage image in Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with speculation about location

claim: Many vesicles containing EGF-Rh and EGFR-GFP are early/sorting endosomes.
source: Co-staining of these sections with EEA.1 antibody demonstrated that many of these vesicles are early/sorting endosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A

claim: Endosomes containing EGF-Rh and EGFR-GFP were co-labeled with the pY1068 antibody, confirming receptor activity in endosomes.
source: Endosomes containing EGF-Rh and EGFR-GFP were also co-labeled with the pY1068 antibody, confirming receptor activity in endosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B

claim: EGFR is capable of rapid internalization in the majority of cells in tumor xenografts in the presence of low concentrations of endogenous and exogenous EGFR ligands.
source: Collectively, these data (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2) show that EGFR is capable of rapid internalization in the majority of cells in tumor xenografts in the presence of low concentrations of endogenous and exogenous EGFR ligands.
evidence: Inferred from data in Figure 6 and supplements

claim: Gefitinib treatment resulted in a strong inhibition of EGF-Rh endocytosis as evidenced by the dramatic reduction in the proportion of cells with detectable EGF-Rh/EGFR-GFP-containing endosomes.
source: Gefitinib treatment resulted in a strong inhibition of EGF-Rh endocytosis as evidenced by the dramatic reduction in the proportion of cells with detectable EGF-Rh/EGFR-GFP-containing endosomes when compared to vehicle-treated tumors (Figure 7).

claim: In vivo EGFR endocytosis is receptor-kinase-dependent.
